claims.text: A high-entropy alloy will exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition under systematic temperature variation.
Molecular dynamics simulations combined with temperature-dependent experiments can demonstrate the proposed ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
The proposed transition occurs because high-entropy alloys inherently resist temper embrittlement.
The relevant temperatures lie within the narrow temperature window in which conventional alloys undergo temper embrittlement.
The complex, multicomponent crystal structure of the high-entropy alloy is the structural mediator.
A high-entropy alloy can maintain ductility across a wide temperature range.
A high-entropy alloy can maintain ductility within the narrow temperature window in which conventional alloys lose ductility.
The high-entropy alloy will have 30% greater ductility than conventional alloys within the temper-embrittlement temperature window.
The predicted 30% ductility increase will have a standard deviation of 5%.
Conventional alloys exhibit temper embrittlement and provide the baseline for comparison.
The exact alloy composition may affect resistance to temper embrittlement and the ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
Processing conditions may affect resistance to temper embrittlement and the ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
A ductility decrease greater than 20% within the specified temperature window would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: A ductile–brittle–ductile transition requires an intermediate brittle or substantially reduced-ductility regime, whereas the proposed mechanism says the alloy resists embrittlement and maintains ductility throughout the relevant temperature range.

The predicted outcome specifies only greater ductility relative to conventional alloys within one temperature window; it does not specify the decrease and subsequent recovery needed to establish a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
